title: The benefit of the doubt
hook: judge others on the side of merit

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: kin'ah, envy. Your line was envy removes. Which way did your envy point? Today, a habit of mind that changes how other people look to you. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-eight.

A worker has labored for a landowner for years. On the eve of Yom Kippur he says: pay me, so I can go home and feed my wife and children. Says the landowner: I have no money. Then give me produce. I have none. Land? None. Cattle? None. Bedding? None. The worker swings his bag over his shoulder and walks home with nothing, sad. The Talmud tells this story in tractate Shabbat, and the part it cares about hasn't happened yet. It's what goes on in the worker's head on the long walk home.
screen: `PAY ME, I'M GOING HOME.` → `NO MONEY, NO LAND, NO CATTLE.` → `A LONG WALK HOME.`

segments.voice: Dan l'kaf zechut. Judging on the side of merit. Turn it four ways. First, the end of the story. After the festival, the landowner shows up at the worker's door with his wages and with donkeys loaded with food and drink and good things. They eat together. Then the landowner asks: when I said I had nothing, what did you suspect? And the worker has an answer for every refusal. No money? I thought you'd found a bargain and spent it. No cattle? I thought they were hired out to others. No land? I thought it was leased. Every time, he picked an innocent explanation. And for the bedding he guessed that the landowner had vowed all his property to Heaven. That was exactly what had happened, and the sages had since released the vow. Then he says the line: as you judged me on the side of merit, may God judge you on the side of merit. Second, the source of the phrase. In Pirkei Avot, Joshua ben Perachiah teaches: judge every person on the side of merit. The picture is a scale. Kaf is the pan of a balance. When the evidence could tip either way, you put your hand on the good side. Third, the Torah. Leviticus says, "in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour," and the Talmud reads that verse as this same instruction: lean toward merit. Fourth, the limits. Commentators on Avot say this applies most to someone you don't know well, or someone whose record is good. It isn't a demand to ignore a pattern. It's a refusal to write the worst story first, when you were only handed half of one.
screen: `WHAT DID YOU SUSPECT?` · `KAF: THE PAN OF A SCALE.` · `IN RIGHTEOUSNESS SHALT THOU JUDGE.` · `NOT BLIND, JUST NOT WORST-FIRST.` · then, large: `THE BENEFIT OF THE DOUBT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: assume the best of one person. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who did something lately that bothered you. An unanswered message. A short tone. A friend who didn't show. Notice the story you've already told yourself about why. Now be the worker on the long walk home. Find one innocent explanation. Then another. They were drowning at work. They didn't see it. Something happened at home they haven't mentioned. You don't have to know which one is true. Just let the scale move. Rest your hand on the side of merit and breathe there for a while. If you pray, you can ask in your own words to judge the way you hope to be judged. The bell holds the time.
Dan l'kaf zechut. Judging on the side of merit: when it could go either way, tipping the scale toward the good. From Pirkei Avot. Today's word.
Your line: the benefit of the doubt. Today, the first time someone lets you down, find one innocent explanation before you decide what it means. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Jews study Joshua ben Perachiah's teaching in Pirkei Avot to judge every person on the side of merit, and the Talmud's story of the worker and the landowner is often retold to illustrate it.

myth: the worker suspected the landowner of cheating him
for every refusal he chose an innocent explanation.
one of the worker's innocent guesses turned out to be exactly true
he guessed the landowner had vowed all his property to Heaven, and he had; the vow was later released.
judging toward merit means ignoring every pattern
commentators apply it most to strangers or people with a good record: not worst-first, not blind.

fork.setup: you're the worker. after years of labor, your employer says he has no money, no land, no cattle. you walk home with nothing. what do you think?
options: there must be an innocent reason.
fork.reveal: he judged on the side of merit at every step, and the landowner blessed him: as you judged me favorably, may God judge you favorably.

original.note: Hebrew: judging toward the pan of merit, from Avot 1:6.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice and don't judge.
what it means: when it could go either way, tip the scale toward the good explanation.
what a scholar hears: kaf is the pan of a balance; Avot 1:6 and the Talmud's reading of Leviticus 19:15 make favorable judgment a duty, while commentators set its limits.

sources.quoted: in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour

notes: Shabbat 127b story retold without the number of years (the Talmud says three years); details of the requests (money, produce, land, cattle, bedding/pillows) and the worker's explanations are paraphrased and partly abridged. Confirm, including that the landowner 'had vowed all his property to Heaven' and the sages released the vow.
Avot 1:6 (Joshua ben Perachiah) paraphrased. 'Kaf is the pan of a balance' is a standard reading of the phrase; confirm.
Leviticus 19:15 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording. Shevuot 30a reading of the verse as 'judge your fellow favorably' (b'tzedek tishpot amitecha); confirm.
The limits (applies most to an unknown person or one with a good record) follow commentators such as Maimonides on Avot 1:6; given as 'commentators'. Confirm.

Editor: corrected 'the truth was even more innocent than his guesses'. In Shabbat 127b the worker's guess for the bedding (all property vowed to Heaven) is exactly what happened; the teach and the matching myth item now say so.
